primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Sitosterolemia due to ABCG5/ABCG8 loss of function
mechanism: ABCG5 and ABCG8 form an ATP-binding cassette sterol-export heterodimer in intestinal enterocytes and hepatocytes. Loss of function reduces efflux of plant sterols back into the intestinal lumen and into bile, increasing dietary plant-sterol absorption and reducing biliary excretion, with systemic sterol accumulation.
vignette: A 15-year-old girl has tendon xanthomas and unexpectedly high plasma plant sterol concentrations despite only modest dietary cholesterol intake. She has intermittent hemolytic anemia with abnormal platelet morphology. Her parents are unaffected. Genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in ABCG8.
lead: Which of the following transport abnormalities most directly explains this patient's disorder?
correct: Reduced export of absorbed plant sterols from enterocytes back into the intestinal lumen and reduced hepatobiliary sterol secretion
distractors: Failure of intestinal NPC1L1-mediated uptake of dietary cholesterol and plant sterols
Failure of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein to lipidate nascent apolipoprotein B
Failure of lysosomal cholesterol export through NPC1 in peripheral cells
Reduced LDL-receptor-mediated uptake of circulating LDL particles by hepatocytes
distractor_notes: Reducing NPC1L1-mediated sterol uptake would decrease rather than increase absorption of plant sterols.
MTTP deficiency causes abetalipoproteinemia with defective ApoB-containing lipoprotein assembly rather than selective plant-sterol accumulation.
NPC1 deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease type C with lysosomal cholesterol trafficking defects and a different neurologic/visceral phenotype.
LDL-receptor deficiency causes familial hypercholesterolemia but does not explain markedly elevated plant sterols and ABCG8 variants.
key_expl: ABCG5 and ABCG8 form sterolin half-transporter heterodimers highly expressed in intestine and liver. They limit retention of dietary plant sterols by exporting them from enterocytes back into the gut lumen and from hepatocytes into bile. Loss of either transporter increases plant-sterol absorption and decreases biliary excretion, causing sitosterolemia, which can manifest with xanthomas, premature atherosclerosis, and hematologic abnormalities.
objective: Explain sitosterolemia as ABCG5/ABCG8 failure of intestinal and hepatobiliary sterol efflux.
